topics.title: Accountability Basics: Scope, Autonomy, and Governance
topics.summary: Accountability means answering for what you do, decide, and fail to do. Learn its standards, five components, how nurses are socialized, and the forces shaping practice.
objectives: You can tell accountability apart from responsibility, authority, and liability.
You can explain top-of-license practice, autonomy, and who sets nursing standards.
You can match a nurse’s behavior to one of the five components.
You can describe how students are socialized into nursing.
You can name six factors that shape nursing practice and accountability.
You can pick the accountable action when pressure conflicts with client safety.
topics.bigPicture:
Accountability is one simple promise: “I will answer for what I do, what I decide, and what I fail to do.” You may need to explain a choice to the client, your employer, the board of nursing, or a court. It is about ownership, not blame.

This idea sits under most Management of Care questions on the NCLEX. You can hand a task to someone else. You cannot hand off your judgment or your duty to follow up. This lesson covers the key words, standards of care, top-of-license practice, autonomy, governance, and the five components. It ends with how students become nurses and the outside forces that change nursing.
recap: Accountability: answering for the outcomes of your judgments, actions, and omissions. Responsibility: the duty that comes with your role.
You can delegate a task, never your accountability. You may also answer for students and trainees you supervise.
Top of license means your full education and legal scope—never beyond scope or competence.
Standards come from the ANA, The Joint Commission, the NLN, state Nurse Practice Acts, and codes of ethics. Policy can narrow scope, never widen it.
Autonomy: nursing regulates itself, and you act within scope. Governance gives nurses control over practice, discipline, and working conditions.
Five components: education, body of knowledge, service orientation, code of ethics, and autonomy through professional organizations.
Socialization thrives with transparency, no blame, best-practice guidelines, and staff input.
Six factors: economics, consumer demand, science and technology, information and telecommunication, legislation (PSDA), and workforce capacity.

keyTerms.def: Answering for your own nursing judgments, actions, omissions, and their results. It cannot be passed to someone else.
The specific duty that comes with your role. A task can be assigned or delegated.
The rightful power to act or direct others, from your license and job position.
Legal responsibility for harm, decided after the fact by a court or board.
Practicing to the full extent of your education, skills, and legal scope (IOM 2010, The Future of Nursing).
What a nurse may legally do, set by the state Nurse Practice Act and board of nursing rules.
Nursing’s power to regulate itself: set standards, write policy, and define scope through state boards.
Your freedom to act within scope, while answering for your actions and advocating for safe care.
Structure from professional organizations that lets nurses control their practice, self-discipline, and working conditions.
The state law that defines nursing, sets legal scope, and creates the board of nursing.
The state agency that licenses, writes rules, investigates, and disciplines nurses to protect the public.
Care that blends the best research, your expertise, and the client’s values.
Professional guidelines that say what a nurse should and should not do.
What every US RN answers for. Standards of Practice follow the nursing process; Standards of Professional Performance cover professional behavior.
Accredits hospitals and other healthcare organizations; its standards focus on the organization.
A national nursing organization focused on nursing education.
Quality and Safety Education for Nurses: a national initiative to improve quality and safety.
Learning to be a member of a group and its rules. In nursing, learning to act, feel, and see the world as nurses do.
Looking back on an experience or mistake to learn from it and its consequences.
A 1990 federal law: adults get written information at admission on their right to accept or refuse care and to make advance directives.
A written statement of the care a person wants, or who decides, if they cannot speak for themselves.

sections.heading: What is accountability?
sections.keyIdea: Accountability means you answer for your judgments, actions, and omissions—and you cannot hand it to anyone else.
sections.body:
Your slides define accountability as being answerable for the outcomes of a task or assignment. You answer for your own actions. You may also answer for the actions of people you supervise or train, such as students or orientees.

Responsibility is different. It is the specific duty that comes with the role you hold. Accountability covers what you fail to do, too. A missed step is an omission, and it counts.

Two more look-alike words are added here for the NCLEX. Authority is the right to act or direct others. Liability is legal blame for harm, decided later by a court or board.

A task can be handed off, but accountability for nursing judgment stays with the licensed nurse. If an assistant takes vital signs, the RN still gives clear directions and acts on the results. “I delegated it” is not a defense.

Your first duty is to the client. You also answer to yourself, the profession, your employer, and the law. When these conflict, client safety wins.

rows: Specific duty that comes with your role
Right to act or direct others
Answering for the outcomes of a task or assignment
Decided later by a court or board

check.q: An assistant charts a postoperative BP of 84/50 but tells no one. Two hours later the client is drowsy and hypotensive. Who was accountable for acting on it?
check.a: The RN keeps accountability for follow-up. The assistant was responsible, and accountable, for reporting the value as directed. The RN was accountable for clear reporting rules, checking results, and acting. Delegation moves the task, not the RN’s accountability.

bullets: Your sense of accountability guides your performance, and your performance shapes client outcomes.
Accountability needs clear, accepted standards of care.
It shapes how you respond to errors and file incident reports.
Own successes and errors. Honoring what went well matters as much as fixing mistakes. It keeps the culture positive.
QSEN (Quality and Safety Education for Nurses) is a national initiative to improve quality and safety.
sections.source: Accountability slides 3–4; authority and liability added for the NCLEX

sections.heading: What is top-of-license practice?
sections.keyIdea: Top-of-license practice means doing all the nursing work your education and legal scope allow—never less, and never more.
sections.body:
Top-of-license (TOL) practice is an interprofessional way of delivering care. It lets nurses practice to the fullest extent of their education, knowledge, skills, and legal scope. It also requires nurses to be accountable in practice. It grew from the Institute of Medicine’s 2010 report, The Future of Nursing: Leading Change, Advancing Health.

Why does it matter? When RNs spend the shift on tasks others could do, RN-only work gets skipped. That includes assessment, teaching, care coordination, and evaluation. The course says TOL covers eight core nursing responsibilities. Two examples are outcomes-focused care and helping clients make safe transitions, such as handoffs and discharges.

TOL includes a duty to advocate for your own and colleagues’ autonomy. It also has two ceilings: your legal scope and your personal competence. Practicing at the top of your license is the opposite of practicing beyond it.

Course vs current: Your course guide limits TOL to nurses with a BSN or higher. Current standard: the 2010 report says every nurse should practice to the full extent of his or her own education and training. Course exam: BSN wording. NCLEX: any RN.
sections.example: RNs spend each morning restocking carts while clients wait for reassessment after opioids. A TOL-minded nurse brings data to the practice council and asks that support staff restock.

check.q: Which reflects TOL practice: passing every meal tray yourself, or coordinating discharge teaching for a client going home on new insulin?
check.a: Coordinating discharge teaching. Safe transitions and teaching need RN judgment. Others can pass trays.

sections.source: Module 42 study guide, p. 2703 (Glossary term 1)

sections.heading: What does autonomy mean in nursing?
sections.keyIdea: The profession regulates itself, and each nurse acts independently within scope—both must answer for their choices.
sections.body:
Autonomy means independence. In nursing it works at two levels.

Professional autonomy belongs to nursing as a whole. The profession regulates itself. It sets standards of practice for its members and writes nursing policy. It holds legal authority, vested in state boards of nursing, to define its goals, roles, and scope of practice. Nursing’s status as a profession depends on this: making its own policy and controlling its own work.

Individual autonomy is yours at the bedside. You may perform needed nursing actions within scope, like repositioning, teaching, or holding an opioid when breathing is slow. You also advocate for safe, evidence-based care. Freedom comes paired with answerability. The more you decide, the more you must explain and document.

On the NCLEX, autonomy appears as the option where the nurse acts within scope instead of waiting for permission.
sections.analogy: A sports league writes the rulebook and disciplines players. That is professional autonomy. Each player chooses how to play within the rules and answers for each play. That is individual autonomy.

rows: Standards, policy, and discipline through boards
Nursing judgments and actions within scope
Scope, competence, medical orders, and the client’s own choices

check.q: A client is hard to arouse with a respiratory rate of 9 after an opioid. The next dose is due. What shows accountable individual autonomy?
check.a: Hold the dose, stimulate and reassess breathing and sedation, follow the respiratory depression protocol, notify the provider, and document.

sections.source: Module 42 study guide, p. 2703 (Glossary term 2); Accountability slide 9

sections.heading: Who sets the rules and standards?
sections.keyIdea: National groups set standards of care, state law sets legal scope, and governance lets nurses control their own practice.
sections.body:
Standards of practice, also called standards of care, are professional guidelines. They spell out what a nurse should and should not do. National groups give this guidance as benchmarks for client care, standards of nursing practice, and codes of ethics.

Your slides name three organizations that set standards: The Joint Commission, the American Nurses Association (ANA), and the National League for Nursing (NLN). Each state also has a Nurse Practice Act to regulate practice.

Governance is the structure that lets nurses run their own professional affairs. Per the course, professional nursing organizations provide it. It sets up social, political, and economic arrangements so nurses control their practice, self-discipline, and working conditions.

Added for the NCLEX: governance works at state, national, and facility levels. At work, shared governance councils let bedside nurses help shape policy. The board decides what is legal. Facility policy can be stricter than the law, but never looser. To change a unit practice, bring evidence to the practice council. Do not quietly ignore policy.

rows: Group of boards; writes the NCLEX and model rules
Code of Ethics; Scope and Standards of Practice
Ethical duty; what every RN must do
Local rules; may be stricter than law
How a task is done here

check.q: Nurses on a unit co-sign wastes they did not witness “to save time.” What should a new nurse do?
check.a: Refuse to co-sign, since that is falsification and a diversion risk. Follow policy, then raise the issue with the manager and practice council.

bullets: ANA Standards of Practice describe what US RNs are accountable for. They follow the nursing process: assessment, diagnosis, outcomes identification, planning, implementation, and evaluation.
ANA Standards of Professional Performance cover how you act as a professional. Examples are ethics, communication, collaboration, leadership, education, and quality of practice.
The Joint Commission (TJC) accredits hospitals and other healthcare organizations. Its standards, such as the National Patient Safety Goals, focus on the organization.
NLN focuses on nursing education and the faculty who teach it.
sections.source: Accountability slides 3, 5, and 9; Module 42 study guide, p. 2703 (Glossary term 3); table and ANA standards list added for the NCLEX

sections.heading: What are the five components?
sections.keyIdea: Five components make nursing an accountable profession: education, a body of knowledge, service, a code of ethics, and professional organization.
sections.body:
The course names five components that promote professional accountability. Exam stems describe a behavior and ask which component it shows. So learn what each one looks like.

The course guide labels component 1 “Education (Body of Knowledge)” and component 2 “Body of Knowledge.” Treat them as two items: learning that gets you licensed, and the knowledge base of the profession.

The slides group them a bit differently (slide 7). They join education and knowledge into one item: finishing a program that gives you the body of knowledge for the role. They then list autonomy and membership in a professional organization as two items. Same ideas, different grouping.

Course vs current: Your course guide says nursing’s codes of ethics are regulated with state boards through the NCSBN. Current standard: the ANA writes the Code of Ethics, and boards enforce the law. Entry routes are compared in the last section.

Course vs current: Your course guide also says Magnet hospitals require BSN-prepared nurses. Current standard: Magnet requires a BSN or higher for nurse managers and leaders, not every staff RN. On a course exam, expect “Magnet requires BSN nurses.” The NCLEX rarely tests it.
bullets: Education. Entry needs an approved nursing program plus passing the NCLEX. The course lists five program types: hospital diploma, associate degree (ADN), bachelor’s (BSN), master’s (MSN), and doctorate (DNP or PhD). The ANA recommends the BSN for entry into professional practice, and the course says Magnet hospitals require BSN-prepared nurses. Many ADN nurses go on through RN-to-BSN programs. Seen as: starting an RN-to-BSN program or earning a certification.

Body of knowledge. Nursing’s own distinct, ever-growing knowledge, built on nursing frameworks and ongoing research. Nurses apply it through evidence-based practice (EBP) to keep care safe. Seen as: checking current evidence before changing a routine.

Service orientation. Unlike jobs driven by profit, nursing puts service to others first, based on tradition and accountability. Rules, policies, and codes of ethics guide it. Seen as: volunteering in a state or national Medical Reserve Corps during a crisis like COVID-19. Volunteers help local health departments with data collection, phone banks, and public health information.

Code of ethics. Respecting the inherent worth and dignity of all people. Doing what is right, even at personal cost, to keep your moral integrity. Nursing has its own profession-specific code. Codes change as society’s needs and values change. Seen as: reporting your own error.

Autonomy and membership in a professional organization. Working under professional groups gives nursing governance, self-regulation, and legal and clinical autonomy. Seen as: joining a specialty association or practice council.
steps: Underline the behavior in the stem.
Ask what drives it: learning, evidence, serving others, doing right at a cost, or shaping standards.
Avoid traps: habit is not a body of knowledge, and paid overtime is not service orientation.
sections.example: Near the end of her shift, a nurse realizes she missed an ordered neurovascular check on a client with a new cast. She does the check now, charts the real time, and tells the charge nurse. She never charts it as done on time.

check.q: A nurse’s friend and coworker smells of alcohol and slurs words while preparing medications. What does the code of ethics require?
check.a: Protect clients first. Stop her from giving care and tell the charge nurse or supervisor right away. Friendship does not outweigh client safety.

sections.source: Module 42 study guide, pp. 2703–2704; Accountability slides 6–9

sections.heading: Why habit is not a defense
sections.keyIdea: You cannot defend a decision based on habit; accountable nurses use current evidence and change practice through proper channels.
sections.body:
You cannot answer for a decision you cannot explain. “We have always done it this way” is not an explanation.

Nursing has a distinct body of knowledge that keeps growing through ongoing research. So some of what you learn now will become outdated.

Your slides tie this component to evidence-based practice (EBP) based on current research. EBP brings new knowledge to the bedside. It blends research, your expertise, and the client’s values. If a unit routine conflicts with evidence, bring the evidence to the practice council or educator. Do not keep it up blindly or change it alone. If an order conflicts with evidence, clarify it with the prescriber.
bullets: Strongest evidence: systematic reviews and meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials.
Next: single randomized trials, then nonrandomized and observational studies.
Then: qualitative and descriptive studies.
Weakest: expert opinion and committee reports.

check.q: Which statement shows accountability for the body of knowledge? (a) “I learned it in school, so it is still right.” (b) “Policy says this, but I’ll check if the evidence changed and bring it to the council.”
check.a: (b). It follows policy while using EBP and governance to update practice.

sections.source: Accountability slide 8; Module 42 study guide, p. 2703 (body of knowledge); evidence ranking added for the NCLEX

sections.heading: What is socialization to nursing?
sections.keyIdea: Socialization is how you learn to think, act, and feel like a nurse, and it works best in an open, blame-free culture.
sections.body:
Entering a profession is like moving into a new society. Socialization is the process of learning to be a member of a group. You learn its social rules and how members relate to each other. Traditionally, you learn to behave, feel, and see the world the way others in that role do.

Professional socialization is more complex. You must also understand work cultures that support high performance and safe practice. A high-performance culture is dynamic. It keeps changing as evidence and needs change.

Why does it matter? Students copy the culture around them. A nurse who learns to speak up and report errors keeps clients safer.
bullets: Transparency. Errors, near misses, and results are shared openly.
Avoidance of blame. People report problems without fear, so the team can fix the system.
Use of best-practice guidelines. Care follows current evidence, not habit.
Staff input. Frontline nurses help shape how the unit works.

rows: Clear expectations, follow-through, rewards and consequences
Clear rules for preparation and performance, applied every time
A powerful driver: study groups and peer feedback
Looking back at a mistake to understand its consequences
Building on what the student does well
Student duties in school and in society

sections.example: After nearly giving a held dose, a student writes a short reflection: what happened, why, and what she will do next time. Her plan is to check for holds before pulling medications. She shares it at post-conference so classmates learn too.

check.q: A classmate laughs that she charted vital signs she never took, “like the staff do.” What is going wrong, and what should you do?
check.a: She is being socialized into an unsafe culture. Charting care not done is falsification. Tell her it is not acceptable. If it continues, tell your clinical instructor. Student codes require honesty in school and clinical.

sections.source: Accountability slides 11–12

sections.heading: What forces shape nursing practice?
sections.keyIdea: Money, consumers, technology, information, laws, and staffing all change what nurses do and what they answer for.
sections.body:
Many factors shape nursing. Most also affect the whole healthcare system. The course names six, shown in the table. Technology and telehealth are taught in the Competence lesson.

Economics. Changes in public and private health insurance have changed the demand for nursing care. Care is shifting from inpatient to outpatient settings. Acute care is still the main place nurses work. But more nurses now work in community-based settings. Specialty areas grew to meet client needs. Various models of integrative care aim to better control rising healthcare costs.

Consumer demand. Healthcare consumers are the general public. Their needs drive any market or service. The push for integrative health services comes from more than the need to consolidate and lower costs. It also comes from consumer interest in complementary health approaches. Today’s consumers know more and speak up more, partly because of the internet.

rows: Expect to work in clinics, homes, and community settings too
Ask about complementary therapies; treat clients as partners
Keep learning new equipment and the EHR; protect data
Point clients to reliable sites; protect privacy in telehealth
Give each adult client advance-directive information (PSDA)
Mentor new nurses; support safe staffing

check.q: A client takes turmeric capsules and sees an acupuncturist. How does consumer demand shape your response?
check.a: Ask about and document every complementary approach without judgment. Check for drug interactions and tell the provider. Clients expect to be partners in integrative care.

sections.source: Accountability slides 13–14 (table: slides 13–19)

sections.heading: How do laws and staffing shape nursing?
sections.keyIdea: Health laws like the PSDA add duties nurses carry out, and a short-staffed workforce raises the stakes for every nurse.
sections.body:
Legislation. New health laws change nurses’ work and consumers’ rights. The course example is the Patient Self-Determination Act (PSDA), a 1990 federal law. At admission, all competent adults must be told in writing about their right to accept or refuse medical care. They must also learn their right to make advance directives. In many organizations, nurses are responsible for making sure the facility follows this law and similar rules.

Workforce capacity. RNs are the largest group of healthcare providers. Even so, the supply of nurses is not projected to meet the demand. Fixing it takes teamwork among health systems, policy makers, nursing educators, and professional organizations.
bullets: Shortage of nursing faculty.
Current nurses reaching retirement.
Changing demographics and an aging population.
High turnover rates.

rows: Help students enter and move through programs faster and more efficiently
Recruit young people early in their education
More scheduling flexibility, better rewards for experienced nurses who mentor, more adequate staffing, higher pay

sections.example: Mr. Lewis, 72, is admitted with pneumonia. The nurse gives him written advance-directive information and asks if he has one. He names his daughter as health care power of attorney. The nurse documents it and asks for a copy for the chart.

check.q: A client says he does not want to make an advance directive. Can he still be admitted and treated?
check.a: Yes. The PSDA requires that he be informed, not that he sign one. Care can never depend on whether a client has an advance directive. Document that he got the information and his choice.

sections.source: Accountability slides 17–19

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.keyIdea: When two answers look alike, find the stem clue that shows who owns the decision and what the law allows.
sections.body: These pairs cause most wrong answers.

rows: Responsibility is doing the task. Accountability is answering for the judgment and result.
Standards, policy, or the board = professional. Acting within scope = individual.
A client choosing about their own care = client autonomy.
Councils, boards, professional groups = governance. Schedules and budgets = management.
Top of license vs beyond scope
Needs a medical order or a skill you lack? Out of scope.
“The hospital allows it” never makes an illegal act legal.
Licensing and discipline = board. Ethics code and advocacy = ANA.
TJC = the organization. ANA = what each RN must do.
Every adult is informed. No one must sign a directive to get care.
Socialization = learning the culture. Benner = clinical skill level.

sections.source: Added for the NCLEX — not in course materials (compares terms from Accountability slides 3–17)

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: The NCLEX shows a nurse in a situation and asks which action best shows accountability—it rarely asks for a definition.
sections.body: The NCLEX rarely asks for a definition. It shows a nurse in a situation. Then it asks which action shows accountability, or which statement needs more teaching. Wrong options often sound efficient or loyal. But they hand off ownership, hide information, or follow habit. Test each option with the three filters below.
bullets: Who owns it? The licensed nurse stays answerable.
Is it honest? It discloses, documents truthfully, and reports.
Is the client first, within scope? It protects the client without breaking scope.
steps: Read the stem. A nurse forgot a client’s 0900 oral antihypertensive. At 1300 the BP is 168/96. Which action best shows accountability? (A) Give it now and chart it at 0900. (B) Assess, tell the provider, follow direction, document accurately, and file an event report. (C) Double the next dose. (D) Let the oncoming nurse decide.
What is it asking? How to own a missed dose.
Key cues. A missed dose is an omission. The high BP needs assessment.
Why the others are wrong. (A) is falsification. (C) is unsafe and needs an order. (D) hands off ownership.
The answer is (B). It assesses, tells the truth, stays in scope, and reports.
Strategy. Cross out options that hide, delay, or hand off ownership.
sections.source: Added for the NCLEX — not in course materials

sections.heading: Worked case: Marcus’s busy shift
sections.keyIdea: Accountability covers the routine you question, the step you missed, and the chance to shape practice through governance.
sections.body: Marcus, a new RN, has a busy surgical shift. A coworker says the unit irrigates drains a way Marcus thinks current guidance no longer supports. He gave an IV opioid at 1400 but could not reassess until 1520 due to an admission. The client is comfortable, with pain at 3/10. The manager also asks for practice council volunteers.
steps: Cues. A routine may conflict with evidence. A required reassessment was late—an omission, even with a good outcome.
Drain routine. He follows current policy but looks up the evidence and brings it to the educator or council.
Late reassessment. IV opioids are usually reassessed in about 15–30 minutes. He reassesses now, charts the real time, and reports per policy.
Prevent a repeat. Next time, he asks the charge nurse for help when tasks clash.
Council. Joining shows component 5 and gives his drain question a proper forum.

check.q: What if the client had a respiratory rate of 8 at 1520?
check.a: Safety first: stay, stimulate, support breathing, follow the reversal or rapid response protocol, and notify the provider. Reporting comes after the client is stable.

sections.source: Added: worked example based on Accountability slides 4 and 8–9

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.keyIdea: In North Carolina, the NCBON sets nursing scope, and the RN keeps assessment, planning, evaluation, delegation, and assignment.
sections.body: The NCLEX will not ask NC statute numbers. Use these facts in real NC practice.
bullets: NCBON regulates nursing under the Nursing Practice Act (G.S. 90-171.19 et seq., Chapter 90, Article 9A).
RN rules: 21 NCAC 36 .0224. LPN rules: .0225. The RN is accountable for assessment, planning, evaluation, delegation, and assignment; the LPN works under RN or provider supervision.
The RN delegates tasks, never the nursing process or judgment. NCBON offers scope-of-practice and UAP delegation decision trees.
Facility policy can be stricter than these rules, never broader. NC is a Nurse Licensure Compact state; follow the practice law where the client is.

NCBON uses a Just Culture–based tool: human error, at-risk behavior, or reckless behavior. Diversion, impairment on duty, fraud, boundary violations, and confidentiality breaches go to the Board. NCBON offers alternative-to-discipline programs.

Advance directives: Health Care Power of Attorney (G.S. Chapter 32A, Article 3) and Declaration of a Desire for a Natural Death, the living will (G.S. 90-321). The portable medical order form is the MOST (Medical Orders for Scope of Treatment).
sections.source: Added: North Carolina practice rules — not in course materials

sections.heading: Course source & clinical clarification
sections.body: Source: Module 42 study guide, Glossary terms 1–3 and the five components, pp. 2703–2704. Unit 7 slides: “The Concept of Accountability” deck, slides 2–9 (outcomes, standards, components) and 11–19 (socialization and factors). Added for NCLEX context: look-alike terms, shared governance, board/NCSBN/ANA roles, ANA standards list, and evidence ranking. Learn both where they differ:
bullets: Top-of-license: Your course guide says TOL is for BSN-or-higher nurses. Current standard: every nurse practices to the full extent of his or her own education and scope. Course exam: BSN wording; NCLEX: any RN.

Entry pathways: Your course materials list diploma, ADN, BSN, MSN, and doctorate as ways in. Current standard: first licensure comes through a diploma, ADN, BSN, or entry-level master’s, plus the NCLEX-RN. Course exam: the five-program list; NCLEX: every route ends with the NCLEX-RN.

Codes of ethics: Your course guide says codes are “regulated alongside state boards of nursing via the NCSBN.” Current standard: the ANA writes the Code; boards enforce the law. Course exam: NCSBN wording; NCLEX: the Code belongs to the ANA.

Magnet: Your course guide says Magnet requires BSN-prepared nurses. Current standard: BSN or higher for managers and leaders, plus a plan to grow BSN staff. Course exam: “requires BSN nurses”; rarely on the NCLEX.

PSDA: Your course slides say all competent adults are informed in writing at admission. Current standard: Medicare- and Medicaid-funded facilities inform every adult client; if the client is too ill, family or a surrogate gets it first, and the client once able. Course exam: slide wording; NCLEX: inform every adult, never require a directive.

Standards groups: Your course slides say TJC, ANA, and NLN set standards for nurses. Current standard: TJC’s standards cover organizations; the ANA writes nursing’s practice standards; the NLN focuses on education.
IOM: Your course materials say Institute of Medicine (IOM). Current name: National Academy of Medicine (since 2015). Shortage projections vary by year and state.
sections.source: Module 42 study guide, pp. 2703–2704; Accountability slides 2–19
sections.keyIdea: This lesson follows the Module 42 study guide and Accountability slides; learn the course wording and the current standard where they differ.

mnemonics.name: Five components: “Every Brave Student Can Achieve”
mnemonics.text: Education • Body of knowledge • Service orientation • Code of ethics • Autonomy and professional organization.

mnemonics.name: Accountable answer pattern: A-A-C-D-R
mnemonics.text: Assess → Act within scope → Communicate → Document truthfully → Report and follow up. Options that skip these steps, hide information, or hand off ownership are usually wrong.

pearls: Delegate tasks, never accountability for your judgment or follow-up.
Omissions count: a missed reassessment or unreported finding is yours to answer for.
Policy can narrow scope but never expand it beyond the Nurse Practice Act.
Change a practice you disagree with through evidence and governance, not quiet noncompliance.
Every adult admitted gets written advance-directive information. Care never depends on having one.
redFlags: Charting care that was not done, or at a false time, is falsification.
Co-signing a waste you did not witness enables drug diversion.
Letting an impaired coworker keep caring for clients violates your first duty to safety.
Assuming a delegated task was done right without checking results.

checks.q: A charge nurse says, “Don’t bother with an event report for that near miss—nothing happened.” What is the accountable response?
checks.a: Explain that near misses are reported so the system can learn and prevent harm. Then file the report per policy.

checks.q: The manager wants a client discharged now for a bed. The client, new on insulin, still cannot inject a dose correctly. What should the nurse do?
checks.a: Say the client cannot inject safely yet, notify the provider, and keep teaching or arrange a safe option. Bed pressure never outweighs safety at discharge.

checks.q: A nurse serves on a specialty association’s standards committee. Which component does this show?
checks.a: Autonomy and membership in a professional organization—taking part in the governance that sets nursing standards.

checks.q: An LPN asks the RN to sign an admission assessment the LPN did alone: “You’re busy; I’ve done hundreds.” Should the RN sign it?
checks.a: No. The comprehensive admission assessment is RN work. The LPN may collect data, but the RN must assess and validate it herself. Signing work she did not do misstates her accountability.

topics.title: Bedside Accountability: Duties, Delegation, Unsafe Orders
topics.summary: At the bedside, accountability means doing your core duties well and keeping the decisions you cannot hand off: delegating safely, questioning unsafe orders, escalating, and owning errors.
objectives: You can apply the six expanded duties to a client situation.
You can decide what to assign, delegate, or keep as the RN.
You can question an unsafe order and escalate it.
You can explain what you answer for with range orders and errors.
You can recognize mandatory reporting and screen for abuse and suicide.
You can match nursing actions to the seven related concepts in the matrix.
topics.bigPicture:
In the first lesson, accountability was a principle. Here it becomes things you do every shift. You assess comfort, screen for abuse and suicide risk, prevent infection, and teach. If you skip one, you answer for the omission.

This lesson also covers decisions under pressure. A client says “I’m fine” while shaking with pain. An LPN throws away urine that was supposed to be strained. An IV order looks unsafe for a 78-year-old. In each case the RN must assess, clarify, speak up, and document. The RN stays accountable for the outcome, even when someone else did the task or wrote the order.
recap: Six duties: wellness, physical outcomes, safety, trauma and suicide, teaching, and infection prevention.
Finish the assessment before leaving the room, especially when words and cues don’t match.
Clarify an order that conflicts with evidence or the client’s condition. Never change it yourself.
If an unsafe order stands: hold it, tell the prescriber, escalate, and document facts.
The RN stays accountable after delegating. Never delegate assessment, teaching, evaluation, or unstable clients to assistive personnel.
You answer for your process—assessing, dosing within the order, monitoring—not for a drug’s biology.
Report suspected abuse without waiting for proof. Screen every client for abuse and suicide risk.
Just Culture: console human error, coach at-risk behavior, sanction reckless behavior.

keyTerms.def: The areas a nurse answers for: wellness, physical outcomes, safety, trauma, education, and infection prevention.
A legal duty to report known or suspected abuse or neglect, and certain injuries such as gunshot wounds, to the agency named in state law.
An infection a client gets while receiving care that was not present or incubating on admission.
Letting someone perform a specific nursing task beyond their usual role. The delegating nurse keeps accountability.
Directing someone to do work within their own scope or routine role, such as an LPN caring for stable clients.
Right task, right circumstance, right person, right directions and communication, and right supervision and evaluation.
Trained, unlicensed staff, such as nursing assistants, who do assigned or delegated tasks under a nurse’s supervision.
The line of authority for an unsolved concern: prescriber, charge nurse, supervisor or manager, then medical director or chief nursing officer.
A report format: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation.
An order with a dose range, such as hydromorphone 1–4 mg IV PRN. The nurse picks the dose by assessment and policy.
A confidential quality-improvement report of an error or near miss. It is never filed in or mentioned in the chart.
A safety approach that consoles human error, coaches at-risk behavior, and disciplines reckless behavior, while fixing system causes.

sections.heading: What duties does accountability cover?
sections.keyIdea: Each duty has an assessment part and an action part, and the right exam answer often adds the skipped assessment.
sections.body:
The course says accountability governs seven areas of care. They are health and wellness needs, physical outcomes, client safety, trauma and abuse reporting, suicide prevention, client teaching, and infection control.

The course groups bedside accountability into six duties. Each has something to assess and something to do. When a question shows a skipped step, it is usually the assessment.

Take education. Before teaching, assess learning style and readiness. Keep your own knowledge current, too.

rows: Body, mind (cognitive and psychologic health), and spirit
Screenings, vaccines, quitting smoking, exercise, healthy diet, stress management; refer to counselor, clergy, or support group
Fluids, nutrition, rest and sleep, oxygenation, elimination, pain and comfort
Meet each need; assess and manage pain proactively; reassess
Hazards in the room; injury risk across the lifespan
Keep the setting hazard-free; teach injury prevention; urge clients to voice concerns
Screen every client for abuse; assess risk of self-harm, suicidal ideation, and intent
Report known or suspected abuse of children and older adults, and violence-related injuries such as gunshot wounds, per state law
Learning style and readiness to learn
Teach about health, illness, tests, procedures, diagnoses, treatments, and self-care; keep up your own continuing education and EBP
Weak immunity; your own exposures and illness
Teach the public about vaccines; prevent healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) with self-awareness of your own exposures and strict infection control

check.q: A client got IV morphine 20 minutes ago, is drowsy, and says, “Just leave the warfarin papers.” Which duty is at risk?
check.a: Education. The client is not ready to learn. Teach when the client is alert, and confirm learning with teach-back.

sections.source: Module 42 study guide, pp. 2703–2704

sections.heading: What does the related-concepts matrix say?
sections.keyIdea: For each related concept, the course lists what the nurse answers for and the exact nursing actions that show it.
sections.body:
The course links seven concepts to accountability in one matrix (p. 2705). The slides list the same seven: comfort, EBP, health and illness, infection, safety, teaching and learning, and trauma. Each row names what you are accountable for. It then lists the nursing actions that prove it. Exam items often describe one of these actions and ask which concept it shows.

Comfort is the row students miss most. You assess comfort, report changes, and document both the comfort level and every intervention.

Course vs current: Your course guide says to assess comfort at least once per shift, or more often if the client’s condition calls for it. Current standard: assess pain on admission, at the intervals set by policy, with any change, and after every pain intervention. On a course exam, expect “at least once per shift.” On the NCLEX, reassess after each intervention.

rows: Assessing comfort and giving effective care to promote it
Assess comfort at least once per shift, or more often per condition; report any change; document comfort level and all interventions
Practicing in an EBP setting and using evidence in your own care
Search the literature for current evidence; choose interventions based on what it shows
Assessing current health and using teaching, care, and referrals to preserve health and prevent illness

Assess biophysical, cognitive, psychologic, and spiritual health; teach general prevention (exercise, vaccines) and risk-specific changes (quit smoking, heart-healthy diet); refer to counselors, clergy, dietitians, physical therapists, support groups, and community resources
Protecting clients whose immune systems are weak and prone to infection
Check history for immune problems (autoimmune disease, cancer, chemotherapy); stay aware of your own health and use PPE; know how diseases spread; teach vaccines and hygiene
Keeping clients safe in care and teaching risk reduction for daily life
Find and fix immediate hazards; assess injury risk outside the facility; report safety concerns to supervisors per policy; teach helmet use and child safety restraints
Client teaching, staying current, and guiding preceptees and students
Assess client and family learning needs and readiness; design teaching from EBP; read current journals and attend workshops or seminars; keep competence through continuing education
Spotting abuse or violence, preventing more harm, and reporting as the law requires
Assess for physical, emotional, or sexual abuse; screen abuse and suicide risk as part of admission; watch for spoken or shown warning signs of abuse or suicide

check.q: A nurse checks a client’s history for chemotherapy and wears PPE. Which matrix concept is this?
check.a: Infection. The nurse is accountable for protecting clients whose immune systems are weak.

sections.source: Module 42 study guide, p. 2705; Accountability slide 10

sections.heading: What if the client says “I’m fine”?
sections.keyIdea: When words and cues don’t match, believe the whole picture, finish the assessment, and keep working on the problem.
sections.body:
In the course case, new RN Jen Sturges assesses Kathryn Miller, 45. She has a GI diagnosis and a history of back pain. Ms. Miller says she is “doing just fine.” But her blood pressure is high, and she is shaking and gripping the sheets. She fears narcotics and “refuses to pay attention to my body.” The shaking and gripping are nonverbal signs of severe pain.

Jen must finish the assessment before leaving the room. Then she reports the findings to the charge nurse.

A competent adult may refuse an opioid. But respecting a refusal is not dropping the problem. Untreated pain raises blood pressure, slows healing, and worsens anxiety. So the nurse explores fears, teaches about non-opioid and nondrug options, and advocates for safe relief. Added: correct myths, too. One myth is that short-term opioid use for acute pain almost always causes addiction.
steps: Notice that the words and cues don’t match.
Finish the assessment: pain scale, nonverbal signs, vital signs, and fears.
Explore: “Tell me more about your fear of narcotics.”
Plan with the charge nurse, provider, and pharmacist (for non-opioid options safe with her GI problem).
Offer options she accepts, and respect an informed refusal.
Reassess after each step. Document comfort, her words, teaching, and interventions.

check.q: After teaching, Ms. Miller still declines all opioids. Is charting “client refuses pain medication” enough?
check.a: No. Charting is required but not enough. Offer ordered non-opioid and nondrug options, tell the provider pain is uncontrolled, and reassess soon.

sections.source: Module 42 study guide, p. 2704 (Case Study Part 1); steps partly added

sections.heading: What if an order seems unsafe?
sections.keyIdea: Clarify before you carry it out; if the prescriber won’t change an unsafe order, hold it and move up the chain of command.
sections.body:
In the course case, Frank Epworth, 78, has a suspected kidney stone. Orders include normal saline at 500 mL/hr. The nurse recalls guidance that large fluid pushes rarely help stones pass. At 78, he also risks fluid overload.

She cannot ignore the concern because “the provider ordered it.” She also cannot change the rate on her own. She questions the order. She calls the prescriber to share the evidence and advocates for a safer, evidence-based rate.

The ANA Code of Ethics backs this up. Your primary commitment is to the client. You must protect the client’s health and safety, and you answer for your own judgments and actions. So if a prescriber refuses to change an unsafe order, refuse to carry it out. That is accountability, not insubordination. Document the conversation. Then go up the chain of command right away: charge nurse, nursing supervisor, then medical director.

Added for the NCLEX: use the TeamSTEPPS tool CUS: “I am Concerned. I am Uncomfortable. This is a Safety issue.” Under the two-challenge rule, say it twice, then move up the chain. Anyone may “stop the line”—pause care—for safety.
steps: Assess the client. For fluids, check lungs, breathing, SpO2, edema, and intake and output.
Check facts with a guideline, drug reference, or pharmacist.
Call the prescriber using SBAR and make a clear recommendation.
If the order changes, read it back and carry it out. If it stays unsafe, hold it and tell the prescriber.
Escalate: charge nurse, supervisor or manager, then medical director or chief nursing officer.
Keep the client safe. Document who, when, what was said, and what was done.

check.q: A provider orders potassium chloride 20 mEq IV push: “Just push it slowly.” What should the nurse do?
check.a: Withhold it, tell the provider, and notify the charge nurse. IV push potassium can cause fatal dysrhythmias.

sections.source: Module 42 study guide, p. 2710 (Case Study 2, Q3; Review & Relate Q5–6); CUS and steps added for the NCLEX

sections.heading: What can you delegate or assign?
sections.keyIdea: The task moves to someone else, but the RN’s accountability for the decision, directions, and follow-up stays put.
sections.body:
In the Epworth case, an LPN says, “He voided 30 mL. I charted it and threw it out without straining.” Is the RN accountable? Yes. The LPN answers for doing the task properly. The RN keeps overall accountability for outcomes, proper delegation, clear directions, and supervising and evaluating the care.

The 2019 NCSBN and ANA guidelines use two terms. Assignment is work within a person’s scope or routine role, like an LPN caring for stable clients. Delegation is a specific nursing task beyond the person’s usual role, after training. The RN stays accountable in both. The steps follow the five rights.

Course vs current: Your course guide says the RN “delegates” urine straining to the LPN. Current standard: under the 2019 NCSBN and ANA guidelines, giving an LPN routine work within LPN scope is an assignment. On a course exam, expect the word “delegates.” On the NCLEX, call it an assignment. Either way, the RN stays accountable.
steps: Right circumstance: Is the client stable and predictable? If new or changing, keep the client.
Right task: Does it need assessment, planning, first teaching, evaluation, or judgment? Then keep it.
Right person: Is it in their scope or task list, allowed by policy, with skill verified?
Right directions: Say what to do and what to report right away. “Strain every void, save any stone in the labeled cup, and tell me at once about clots or new pain.”
Right supervision: Check in, review results yourself, act, and give feedback.

check.q: Which can go to a nursing assistant: teaching insulin injection, a fingerstick glucose on a stable client, or a fresh post-op assessment?
check.a: The fingerstick, if it is on the approved list and skill is verified. The others stay with the RN.

sections.source: Module 42 study guide, p. 2710 (Case Study 2, Q1); 2019 NCSBN/ANA guidelines and five rights added for the NCLEX

sections.heading: What do you answer for with medications?
sections.keyIdea: You are not accountable for how a drug works in the body, but you are accountable for every step of your process.
sections.body:
Mr. Epworth’s order is hydromorphone (Dilaudid) 1–4 mg IV PRN (as needed). An hour after 1 mg, his pain is still 8/10, so the nurse gives 3 mg. Is she accountable if it fails? Not for the drug’s failure. She is accountable for her process.

First, check the order and the policy on choosing a dose within a range. Assess pain, sedation, breathing, and SpO2. Older adults have higher risk of slowed breathing, so watch closely. Reassess at peak, often about 15–30 minutes for IV opioids. Call the provider if relief is poor. Sedation rises before breathing slows, so growing sleepiness is a warning.

You also own your errors. Assess and treat the client first. Then notify the provider, chart the facts, and file an event report. Never mention the report in the chart.

Just Culture judges the choice behind an error, as the table shows.

rows: Picking the wrong client from look-alike names
Skipping barcode scanning because it is slow

sections.example: Thirty minutes after 3 mg, Mr. Epworth is drowsy but easy to wake. Respirations are 14 and pain is 5/10. The nurse keeps watching and calls the provider about a non-opioid. Before any NSAID, she checks kidney function, bleeding risk, and GI history.

check.q: Is the nurse accountable for the drug failing to relieve pain, or for the 30-minute reassessment?
check.a: The reassessment and what follows. Nurses answer for a sound process, not for a client’s drug response.

sections.source: Module 42 study guide, p. 2710 (Case Study 2, Q2); Accountability slide 4 (errors and incident reporting); Just Culture added

sections.heading: Safety, infection, abuse, and suicide screening
sections.keyIdea: Fix hazards first, protect weak immune systems, screen privately for abuse, ask directly about suicide, and report suspicion.
sections.body:
Safety: fix an immediate hazard first, then report it. Teach prevention, such as bike helmets and child car seats.

Infection: check for weak immunity from cancer, chemotherapy, or autoimmune disease. Know how diseases spread. Use PPE and teach about vaccines and hygiene. Stay aware of your own health. If you have a fever, tell your supervisor and employee health, and stay home.

Abuse: screen every client for abuse as part of admission, in private. Document objective findings and the client’s own words. Report reasonable suspicion. You need no proof, and you do not investigate. Some injuries, such as gunshot wounds, must be reported per state law even if the client objects.

Suicide: screen for suicide risk on admission, too. Stay alert for spoken or shown warning signs. Ask directly, “Are you thinking about killing yourself?” Asking does not plant the idea.

Course vs current: Your course guide says nurses must report known or suspected abuse of children and older adults. Current standard: every state requires reports of suspected child abuse. Adult rules vary by state. In NC, the adult duty covers a disabled adult who needs protective services, not age alone. On a course exam, expect “children and older adults.” On the NCLEX, report suspected abuse of a child or vulnerable adult to the designated agency.

rows: Burns in a pattern that doesn’t fit the story
Keep the child safe; treat; document; report to child protective services
“Everyone would be better off without me”
Ask directly about thoughts, plan, and means; keep safe
Nurse with fever before an oncology shift
Stay home; notify supervisor and employee health

check.q: A woman with a facial bruise says she “walked into a door.” Her partner answers every question. What first?
check.a: Interview her privately with direct, caring screening questions. Safety planning and any required report follow.

sections.source: Module 42 study guide, pp. 2704–2705; staying home with fever and private screening added

sections.heading: Common traps
sections.keyIdea: Most traps hinge on who owns the decision, whether the client is stable, and whether the action is in scope.
sections.body: When two answers both sound right, use this table.

rows: Either way, the RN stays accountable. Match the task to the person and the client’s stability.
Words like evaluate, interpret, or assess mean RN work.
New symptoms or a fresh post-op client stay with the RN.
Never adjust a rate or dose on your own.
Report suspicion. Never wait for proof or confront the suspected abuser.
Never write “incident report filed” in the chart.

sections.source: Added for the NCLEX — not in course materials

sections.heading: How the NCLEX tests this
sections.keyIdea: Expect delegation, unsafe-order, reporting, and error questions; the right answer protects the client and keeps judgment with the RN.
sections.body: Four question types show up often. Delegation asks which task or client fits an LPN or assistant. Unsafe orders ask what the nurse does first. Reporting asks about abuse, suicide, or reportable injuries. Errors ask who is accountable and what to document.
steps: Read the stem. “Which client should the RN assign to the LPN?” (A) Chest pain, admitted 30 minutes ago. (B) Stable chronic leg ulcer needing a scheduled dressing and routine oral meds. (C) Needs first teaching on home tube feeding. (D) Two hours after thyroidectomy with new tingling around the mouth.
What is it really asking? Which client is stable with a predictable outcome.
Key cues. “30 minutes ago,” “first teaching,” and “new tingling” mean RN work. “Stable” and “routine” fit an LPN.
Why (A) is wrong. A new chest-pain admission is not yet stable.
Why (C) is wrong. First teaching belongs to the RN.
Why (D) is wrong. Tingling after thyroid surgery suggests low calcium—an acute change.
The answer is (B). Routine care for a stable client fits LPN scope.
Strategy. Stable and routine can go to others. New, changing, teaching, or assessment stays with the RN.
sections.source: Added for the NCLEX — not in course materials

sections.heading: Worked case: Dana’s night shift
sections.keyIdea: Assess the biggest physical threat first, give clear directions, and report suspected abuse without confronting anyone.
sections.body: Dana, an RN, works nights with an LPN, Rob, and an assistant, Kia. Mr. Ortiz, 81, has heart failure, crackles, and a new order for saline at 250 mL/hr. Rob has Ms. Patel, who has renal colic and an order to strain all urine. Mrs. Greene, 84, has a hip fracture and bruises of different ages on both arms. Her son answers every question and won’t leave.
steps: Prioritize. Fluid overload is the biggest threat. Dana assesses Mr. Ortiz first, then calls the provider with SBAR and suggests a lower rate.
Direct clearly. Rob strains every void and saves any stone. Kia reports Mr. Ortiz’s urine output every 2 hours and any breathing trouble at once.
Screen privately. Dana talks with Mrs. Greene alone and documents the bruises and her words.

Report. She tells the provider and charge nurse and reports to adult protective services per state law (in NC, county DSS under G.S. 108A-102 if she is a disabled adult needing protective services). She does not confront the son or wait for proof.
Evaluate. She rechecks Mr. Ortiz and follows up on the report.

check.q: At 0300, Rob says he forgot to strain one void. Who is accountable?
check.a: Both. Rob answers for his work; Dana answers for supervision and the outcome. She reinforces directions, tells the provider if it matters, documents, and gives feedback without blame—a human error.

sections.source: Added: worked example based on Module 42 study guide, pp. 2704–2710

sections.heading: Worked case: Ms. Miller’s hidden pain
sections.keyIdea: Finish the assessment, trust the cues over “I’m fine,” report the full picture, and keep working when a client refuses pain medicine.
sections.body:
This is the course’s Case Study Part 1 (p. 2704). New RN Jen Sturges assesses Kathryn Miller, 45. She was admitted with a GI diagnosis and has a history of back pain. The nursing assistant (CNA) took her blood pressure, and it is high.

Ms. Miller says she is “doing just fine.” But she is shaking, very anxious, and gripping the bed sheets tightly. She fears narcotics. She says she “refuses to pay attention to my body” and that “pain is my enemy.” Work through the five course questions below.
steps: Q1. Why finish the assessment before leaving the room? A full assessment catches subtle body and behavior cues, such as high BP, shaking, and guarding. That prevents missed decline. It also meets Jen’s duty to get accurate baseline data and manage comfort.
Q2. What other symptoms does Jen see? High blood pressure (taken by the CNA), extreme anxiety, shaking, tight gripping of the sheets, and spoken denial or avoidance of pain (“pain is my enemy”).

Q3. What should Jen tell the charge nurse? The high BP, the nonverbal signs of severe pain (shaking, gripping sheets), her fear of narcotic side effects, her back pain history, and her GI diagnosis. Then they can plan safe, tailored pain care.

Q4. Who should they work with? The primary healthcare provider (HCP) or hospitalist. The clinical pharmacist, to review non-narcotic or multimodal pain drugs that are safe with her GI problem. Possibly a pain management specialist or a physical or integrative therapist.

Q5. Why not just accept the refusal? Untreated pain causes harmful stress responses: high BP, slower healing, and more anxiety. Accountability for comfort means exploring her fears, teaching about non-opioid and nondrug options, and advocating for safe relief. Accepting the refusal and walking away abandons the problem.

check.q: Ms. Miller says she is fine, but she is shaking and gripping the sheets. What should Jen do before leaving the room?
check.a: Finish the assessment, including a pain rating, nonverbal signs, vital signs, and her fears. Then report the full picture to the charge nurse.

sections.source: Module 42 study guide, p. 2704 (Case Study Part 1)

sections.heading: Worked case: Mr. Epworth’s kidney stone
sections.keyIdea: The RN answers for delegation choices, her own medication process, and questioning orders that conflict with evidence.
sections.body:
This is the course’s Case Study 2 (p. 2710). Frank Epworth, 78, is admitted with a suspected kidney stone (urolithiasis). He has severe left flank and back pain, nausea and vomiting, and blood in the urine (hematuria).

Orders: Dilaudid (hydromorphone) 1–4 mg IV PRN for pain, normal saline IV at 500 mL/hr, and strain all urine. The RN gives Dilaudid 1 mg IV. She delegates urine collection and straining to an LPN. Work through the three course questions below.
steps: Q1. Thirty minutes later, the LPN says he voided 30 mL five minutes ago. She charted it and threw it out without straining. Is the RN accountable? Yes. The LPN answers for doing the task right. The RN keeps overall accountability for outcomes, proper delegation, clearly stating the key instruction (strain for stone analysis), and supervising and evaluating the care.

Q2. An hour after the first dose, pain is 8/10 with no relief. The RN gives 3 mg more per the order. Is she accountable if it fails? No, not for the drug failing. That holds if she assessed well, gave a dose within the 1–4 mg range safely, and monitored him. She is accountable for reassessing pain afterward and calling the HCP if the plan still fails.

Q3. After starting the IV, she recalls guidance that large fluid pushes rarely help stones pass. What now? Accountability for EBP and safety applies. He is 78, and 500 mL/hr risks fluid overload. She questions the order, calls the prescriber to share the evidence, and advocates for a safer, evidence-based rate.

check.q: Is the RN accountable when the LPN throws away unstrained urine?
check.a: Yes. The LPN answers for the task, but the RN answers for the handoff decision, the clear directions, and the follow-up.

sections.source: Module 42 study guide, p. 2710 (Case Study 2)

sections.heading: North Carolina practice note
sections.keyIdea: In NC, the RN delegates tasks, not judgment, and anyone who suspects child maltreatment must report it to county DSS.
sections.body: Use these NC facts in real practice. The NCLEX tests the national rule: report suspicion to the designated agency.
bullets: Under 21 NCAC 36 .0224 (RN) and .0225 (LPN), the RN is accountable for assessment, planning, evaluation, delegation, and assignment. NCBON publishes a Decision Tree for Delegation to UAP.
Nurse Aide I registry: NC DHHS Division of Health Service Regulation. Nurse Aide II registry: NCBON. NA II must also be on the NA I registry.
NA II tasks include some sterile and advanced tasks, such as sterile dressings and oxygen. The task must be on the list and right for this client.

Children (G.S. 7B-301): anyone who suspects a juvenile under 18 is abused, neglected, or dependent, or died from maltreatment, must report to the county DSS director. Knowingly not reporting is a crime.

Disabled adults (G.S. 108A-102): anyone with reasonable cause to believe a disabled adult needs protective services must report to county DSS. Older adults are covered when they meet this definition. Report suspicion; do not investigate.
Good-faith reporters are immune. A hospital’s internal process does not replace your duty to make sure DSS gets the report.
Diversion, impairment, fraud, boundary violations, and confidentiality breaches go to the Board.
sections.source: Added: North Carolina practice rules — not in course materials

sections.body: Source: Module 42 study guide, “The Concept of Accountability” intro and “Expanded Duties Under Accountability” (pp. 2703–2704), the Nursing Implications Matrix (p. 2705), Case Study 1: Ms. Kathryn Miller (p. 2704), Case Study 2: Mr. Frank Epworth (p. 2710), and “Linking Accountability to Ethics” (p. 2710). Unit 7 slides: “The Concept of Accountability” deck, slide 10 (Concepts Related to Accountability) and slide 4 (accountability shapes the response to errors and incident reporting). Added: NCSBN/ANA (2019) delegation guidelines, CUS, SBAR, and Just Culture.
bullets: Delegation vs assignment: Your course guide says the RN “delegates” straining to an LPN. Current standard: under the 2019 NCSBN/ANA guidelines, that is an assignment. On a course exam, expect “delegates”; on the NCLEX, call it an assignment. The RN is accountable either way.

Comfort checks: Your course guide says assess comfort at least once per shift, or more often per condition. Current standard: also assess on admission, with changes, and after each intervention (about 15–30 minutes for IV and 30–60 minutes for oral). On a course exam, expect “at least once per shift”; on the NCLEX, reassess after every intervention.

Reporting: Your course guide says report abuse of “children and older adults.” Current standard: child reporting is universal, but adult rules vary by state (in NC, disabled adults who need protective services). On a course exam, expect “children and older adults”; on the NCLEX, report suspected abuse of a child or vulnerable adult to the designated agency.
Hydromorphone: 3 mg an hour after 1 mg is fine only if the order’s frequency and policy allow.
Unsafe orders: also tell the prescriber you are holding it, and keep monitoring.
